newsitem.title: UK: G7 gets its way again, but with volatility blushes.
newsitem.headline: G7 gets its way again, but with volatility blushes.

text.p: The collapse of the dollar against the yen since last week should make traders pay more heed to warnings from the Group of Seven industrialised nations (G7) about dislocated exchange rates, analysts said.

Nevertheless, the surge in exchange rate volatility which has accompanied the G7-inspired retreat - the biggest one-week drop in dollar/yen in almost eight years - flies in the face of its mantra about more stable currency rates.
In the short-term at least, the goals of reversing a market trend and calming exchange rates may be mutually exclusive.

Analysts said the authorities - from the U.S., Japan, Germany, Italy, the UK, France and Canada - will tolerate the rise in volatility for now in return for convincing the market its previous dollar direction was fundamentally unsound.

"The market would do well to take more notice of the G7 when their wishes are in line with fundamentals - trade trends, likely movements in interest rate spreads and the sheer weight of market positions," said Nick Parsons, foreign exchange strategist at Banques Paribas.
"The speed of last week's move does run a danger of becoming counter-productive, but we should see some calming comments from officials in the days ahead," said Parsons.

In Washington on April 27, a statement from G7 finance ministers and central bankers said they agreed "exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that excess volatility and significant deviations from fundamentals are undesirable."

The immediate reaction, however, mirrored the aftermath of the Washington G7 meeting in April 1995. Back then, the market's initial failure to acknowledge the G7's desire to boost dollar/yen now seems churlish in the face of the dollar's 60 percent rise over the following two years.

This year the dollar/yen was again oblivious to the G7 statement, which this time was aimed at keeping a lid on the dollar. Instead the U.S. unit pushed even higher the following week and set its strongest level in more than 4-1/2 years.

For the Japanese Ministry of Finance, this was the last straw. Last week they unleashed a barrage of verbal intervention aimed at capping the dollar and raised the prospect of a rise in Japanese interest rates later this year.
"The dollar was far too strong and I don't think we'll see the 127 level for a long time again - if ever," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.

"An even weaker yen does little to help Japan's fragile financial sector but low interest rates do. With inflation already 2-1/2 points above interest rates, a stronger currency is needed to facilitate keeping the these interest rates low."
From a high of 126.82 yen on Tuesday, the dollar lost more than seven yen to a low at 119.00 on Friday afternoon and it lost more than 1-1/2 yen further to 117.60 early Monday.

The implied level of one-month volatility in dollar/yen calculated in the options market surged to 11.50 percent today - almost three full percentage points higher than the week before the G7 meeting.
Options pricing, meantime, is now heavily skewed in favour of further yen strength and shows a market scrambling to hedge against further dollar losses and more volatility.
Some say this sort of volatility is inherent in a currency pair like dollar/yen.

"You simply can't fine-tune an exchange rate that has interest rate differentials this wide," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro. "The G7's 'excess volatility' is code for 'we don't like the direction'. It's almost impossible to stabilise currencies like these."

Even if the authorities convinced the market the exchange rate is going to be stable, then the huge interest rate gap in favour of the dollar -- 400 basis points now on 10-year yields -- makes buying dollars a one-way bet, said Norfield.
To even stabilise the dollar, they have to convince the market that potential dollar losses are at least equal to what you will earn from the interest rate pick up over holding yen.

Moreover, so many funds in recent months had assumed this interest rate gain was free of currency risk that even the slightest change in the risk profile has meant a massive shift of capital against the dollar.
"The G7 may not be omnipotent, but it gets fundamentals right faster than the market," said UBS's Von Maydell.
